:::lede
Section [3.6](/notes/math-55a/3-6-free-groups-and-presentations) introduced free groups (Definition [3.6.6](/notes/math-55a/3-6-free-groups-and-presentations#definition-3-6-6)), presentations $\langle S \mid R \rangle = F(S) / \langle\!\langle R \rangle\!\rangle$ (Definition [3.6.13](/notes/math-55a/3-6-free-groups-and-presentations#definition-3-6-13)), and the standard method for proving that a group has a given presentation: check that the relations hold in the group, which gives a surjection from the presented group (Proposition [3.6.14](/notes/math-55a/3-6-free-groups-and-presentations#proposition-3-6-14)), and then show that this surjection is injective. It also posed the word problem: given two words in the generators of $\langle S \mid R \rangle$, decide whether they represent the same element. For groups whose elements we can compute with directly, such as groups of permutations or of matrices, this is easy: evaluate both words and compare. For a group known only through a presentation it can be hard, and by the Novikov–Boone theorem there are finitely presented groups for which no algorithm solves it.

This chapter develops two tools for understanding a group given by generators and relations. The *Cayley graph* turns the group into a geometric object, and *normal forms* single out a preferred word for each element. We apply them to the symmetric groups, the braid groups, and the groups $\SL_2(\ZZ)$ and $\PSL_2(\ZZ)$.
:::

## <span class="num">12.1.1</span> Definition and First Examples

:::definition{12.1.1} Cayley graph
Let $G$ be a group generated by $g_1, \ldots, g_n$. The ***Cayley graph*** of $G$ with respect to these generators has:

- one vertex for each element of $G$;
- for each $s \in G$ and each generator $g_i$, a directed edge from $s$ to $sg_i$, labeled $g_i$.
:::

Every vertex has one outgoing and one incoming edge with each label. When a generator satisfies $g_i = g_i^{-1}$, the edges $s \to sg_i$ and $sg_i \to s$ come in pairs, and we draw each pair as a single undirected edge. A word $x_1 x_2 \cdots x_k$ in the letters $g_i^{\pm 1}$ describes a path from $e$ to $x_1 \cdots x_k$, following the edge labeled $g_i$ forward for each letter $g_i$ and backward for each letter $g_i^{-1}$. Since the $g_i$ generate $G$, the Cayley graph is connected.

:::note
$G$ acts on its Cayley graph by left multiplication: $g \in G$ sends the vertex $s$ to $gs$ and the edge $s \to sg_i$ to the edge $gs \to gsg_i$, which has the same label. This action is transitive on vertices, and transitive on the edges with a given label, so the Cayley graph looks the same from every vertex.
:::

:::example{12.1.2} Cayley graph of $\ZZ$
With the generator $1$, the Cayley graph of $\ZZ$ is the integer number line:

![fig-12-1-1](/notes/math-55a/figures/fig-12-1-1.svg)
:::

:::example{12.1.3} Cayley graph of $S_3$
Take the generators $s_1 = (1\,2)$ and $s_2 = (2\,3)$. Since $s_i^{-1} = s_i$, we draw undirected edges. The six vertices form a hexagon whose edges are alternately labeled $s_1$ (red) and $s_2$ (blue); next to each vertex we give the permutation in cycle notation.

![fig-12-1-2](/notes/math-55a/figures/fig-12-1-2.svg)

Every vertex has exactly one $s_1$-edge and one $s_2$-edge. The two paths from $e$ to the bottom vertex show that $s_1 s_2 s_1 = s_2 s_1 s_2$; given $s_1^2 = s_2^2 = e$, this relation is equivalent to $(s_1 s_2)^3 = e$, which says that the path $s_1 s_2 s_1 s_2 s_1 s_2$ around the hexagon closes up. In fact $S_3 \cong \langle s_1, s_2 \mid s_1^2, s_2^2, (s_1 s_2)^3 \rangle$, the case $n = 3$ of Theorem [3.6.18](/notes/math-55a/3-6-free-groups-and-presentations#theorem-3-6-18).
:::

:::example{12.1.4} Cayley graph of $S_4$
Take the generators $s_1 = (1\,2)$, $s_2 = (2\,3)$, and $s_3 = (3\,4)$. In the figure, each vertex $\sigma$ is labeled by the string $\sigma(1)\sigma(2)\sigma(3)\sigma(4)$ (the ***one-line notation*** of $\sigma$). The vertex $\sigma s_i$ is obtained from $\sigma$ by swapping the entries in positions $i$ and $i + 1$, since $(\sigma s_i)(i) = \sigma(i+1)$ and $(\sigma s_i)(i+1) = \sigma(i)$. Edges labeled $s_1$, $s_2$, $s_3$ are drawn in red, blue, and green, and edges at the back are dashed.

![fig-12-1-3](/notes/math-55a/figures/fig-12-1-3.svg)

The 24 vertices and 36 edges form the edges of a truncated octahedron, also called the ***permutohedron***. Its faces correspond to relations. The six squares have edges alternately labeled $s_1$ and $s_3$, and express $s_1 s_3 = s_3 s_1$. The eight hexagons have edges alternately labeled $s_1, s_2$ or $s_2, s_3$, and express $s_1 s_2 s_1 = s_2 s_1 s_2$ and $s_2 s_3 s_2 = s_3 s_2 s_3$. The identity $1234$ is at the bottom and $4321$ at the top; Section [12.2](/notes/math-55a/12-2-permutation-diagrams-and-normal-forms-in-s-n) will show that every edge going up increases the distance from $e$ by one.
:::

## <span class="num">12.1.2</span> Word Length and Growth

:::definition{12.1.5} Word length
Let $G$ be generated by $g_1, \ldots, g_n$. The ***word length*** $\ell(g)$ of $g \in G$ is the distance from $e$ to $g$ in the Cayley graph, where edges may be followed in either direction. Equivalently, $\ell(g)$ is the smallest $k$ such that $g = x_1 x_2 \cdots x_k$ with each $x_j \in \{g_1^{\pm 1}, \ldots, g_n^{\pm 1}\}$.
:::

For finite groups the Cayley graph is finite, but word lengths remain interesting; we study them for $S_n$ in the next section. For infinite groups, the Cayley graph also records how fast the group grows.

:::definition{12.1.6} Growth
Let $G$ be generated by $g_1, \ldots, g_n$, and let $B(N)$ be the number of elements $g \in G$ with $\ell(g) \leq N$. The group has ***polynomial growth*** if there are constants $C$ and $d$ with $B(N) \leq C N^d$ for all $N \geq 1$, and ***exponential growth*** if there are constants $C > 0$ and $c > 1$ with $B(N) \geq C c^N$ for all $N$.
:::

These notions do not depend on the choice of generators. If $g_1', \ldots, g_m'$ is another generating set, with word length $\ell'$ and counting function $B'$, choose $L$ such that each $g_j'^{\pm 1}$ is a product of at most $L$ letters $g_i^{\pm 1}$. Then $\ell(g) \leq L\ell'(g)$, so $B'(N) \leq B(LN)$, and a bound $B(N) \leq CN^d$ gives $B'(N) \leq CL^d N^d$. Exchanging the roles of the two generating sets, with a constant $L'$, gives $B(M) \leq B'(L'M)$ for all $M$; so if $B(N) \geq Cc^N$, then taking $M = \lfloor N/L' \rfloor$, $$B'(N) \geq B(\lfloor N/L' \rfloor) \geq C c^{N/L' - 1} = \tfrac{C}{c} \bigl(c^{1/L'}\bigr)^N.$$

:::example{12.1.7} Growth of abelian and free groups
If $G$ is abelian and generated by $g_1, \ldots, g_n$, every element of word length at most $N$ can be written $m_1 g_1 + \cdots + m_n g_n$ with $|m_1| + \cdots + |m_n| \leq N$, so $B(N) \leq (2N + 1)^n \leq 3^n N^n$: finitely generated abelian groups have polynomial growth. In the free group $F_k$ with $k \geq 2$, distinct reduced words are distinct elements, and the word length of an element is the length of its reduced word. There are $2k(2k-1)^{N-1} \geq 3^N$ reduced words of length exactly $N \geq 1$, so $F_k$ has exponential growth. (The free group $F_1 \cong \ZZ$ has polynomial growth.)
:::

:::note
A deep theorem of Gromov (1981) characterizes polynomial growth: a finitely generated group has polynomial growth if and only if it has a nilpotent subgroup of finite index. Here a group $G$ is *nilpotent* if the sequence $G_1 = G$, $G_{j+1} =$ the subgroup generated by all $ghg^{-1}h^{-1}$ with $g \in G$ and $h \in G_j$, reaches $\{e\}$; abelian groups are the case $G_2 = \{e\}$.
:::
